The invisibility cloak is realized by femtosecond laser direct writing in borosilicate glass.
Up to 5,000 waveguides are printed in a three-dimensional spindle shape to form the cloak.
The hidden inner structure measures about 0.44 mm × 0.35 mm.
Waveguides have a refractive index contrast of 0.0015 relative to the substrate.
The optimal waveguide pitch for cloaking is 21 µm, balancing image clarity and crosstalk.
Normalized cross correlation (Γ) is used to quantify image similarity, reaching a peak value of 0.986 at optimal pitch.
Tomography analysis shows light circumvents the cloaked area along waveguides.
The cloak maintains performance within a viewing angle tolerance of approximately 8.0° laterally and 6.7° vertically.
Phase distortion from waveguide length differences can be minimized by designing length differences as integral multiples of 2π.
A 405 nm Gaussian beam is used for testing the cloak's optical performance.
The cloak is fabricated on a 20 mm × 20 mm × 1 mm borosilicate chip.
Waveguide bending radius is about 85.9 mm to optimize cloaking efficiency.
Crosstalk distortion decreases by about 85% for every 2 µm increase in waveguide pitch.
The cloak can hide millimeter-scale volumes inside a photonic chip.
Image quality benchmarks indicate the cloak can achieve retina-like image clarity.
The printed cloak enables potential on-chip quantum photonic applications such as coupling and swapping operations.
The waveguides guide light with modest curvature to mimic Poynting vector flow in transformation optics.
The spindle cross section size is approximately 0.7 mm × 0.7 mm.
The experimental setup uses CCD cameras and lenses to capture output images and measure viewing angles.
The cloak demonstrates broadband operation and three-dimensional capacity despite being implemented in one dimension experimentally.
